blocks.title: Introduction and Definition
blocks.text:
• All multicellular autotrophic eukaryotic organisms are placed under kingdom plantae.
  • A few exceptions are partially heterotrophs such as insectivorous plants e.g. Bladderwort (Utricularìa) and Venus fly trap plant (Dionaea).
  • Kingdom Plantae includes five divisions such as :
1. Algae

2. Bryophyta

3. Pteridophyta

4. Gymnosperm

5. Angiosperm

blocks.title: Algae
blocks.text:
• Algae are chlorophyll–bearing, simple, thalloid, autotrophic, and largely aquatic (both fresh water and marine) organisms.
  • They occur in a variety of other habitats: moist stones, soils, and wood. Some of them also occur in association with fungi ( lichen) and animals ( e.g. on the sloth bear)

blocks.title: General Character of Algae
blocks.text:
• The plant body of maximum algae is made of haploid cells.
  • Algae are photoautotrophic (Oxygenic phototrophs). They have a plastid in which photosynthetic pigments are present.

blocks.title: Reproduction in Algae
blocks.text:
• All modes of syngamy can be seen in a single genus Chlamydomonas.
  • Sex organs of algae are unicellular and non-jacketed but in Chara, sex organs are multi-cellular and jacketed

blocks.title: Chlorophyceae
blocks.text:
• They are usually grass green due to the dominance of pigments chlorophyll a and b.
  • Green algae are the most advanced algae. It is believed that green algae are the ancestors of the higher plants.
  • Green algae show Haplontic or Zygotic meiosis patterns of the life cycle.
Forms of Green Algae:-

  • Unicellular:      • e.g. Chlamydomonas - Motile unicellular algae. These algae move with the help of flagella.
      • Chlorella – non-motile algae
  • Colonial:      • e.g. Volvox - Motile colony
  • Multicellular filamentous:      • Mostly the green algae are multicellular and filamentous.
      • e.g. Ulothrix, Spirogyra

blocks.title: Phaeophyceae or Brown Algae
blocks.text:
• Habitat: The members of phaeophyceae are found primarily in marine habitats.
  • Brown algae are the largest in size (up to 100 meters in length).
  • Phycocolloids (Algin) protect brown algae against desiccation and shocks. Phycocolloids are used in ice-cream as a thickening agent.
  • Kelps: Profusely branched and giant algae are known as kelps.
General characteristics:-

blocks.title: RHODOPHYCEAE (RED ALGAE)
blocks.text:
• Commonly called red algae because of the predominance of the red pigment r-Phycoerythrin in their body.
  • Red algae are ancient (Primitive) algae.
  • There is no motile stage found in the life cycle of red algae i.e. cilia & flagella are absent.
  • Habitat: The majority of the red algae is mainly found in marine water with greater concentration found in the warmer areas.
  • Agar agar obtained from Gellidium and Gracilaria
General characteristics:-

blocks.title: Example -1
blocks.question:
Q.1 Which one of the following shows isogamy with non-flagellated gametes?

(1) Sargassum

(2) Ectocarpus

(3) Ulothrix

4) Spirogyra
blocks.answer:
Ans-4

Explanation:

  • Isogamy is a type of sexual reproduction where the gametes involved are morphologically similar (same size and shape) but may differ physiologically.
  • Non-flagellated gametes are gametes that lack flagella and cannot move actively.

blocks.question:
Q.2 Male gemetes are flagellated in :

(1) Anabaena

(2) Ectocarpus

(3) Spirogyra

(4) Polysiphonia
blocks.answer:
Ans-2

Explanation:

  • Flagellated male gametes are characteristic of many algae, where the male gametes (sperms) are motile and use flagella for movement.

(1) Volvox

(2) Ulothrix

blocks.answer:
Ans-1

Explanation:

  • Colonial algae are algae that exist in groups or colonies, where individual cells are often specialized for different functions but remain physically connected.

blocks.title: Example-4
blocks.question:
Q.4 Zygotic meiosis is characteristic of;

(1) Fucus

(2) Funaria

(3) Chlamydomonas

(4) Marchantia
blocks.answer:
Ans-3

Explanation:

  • Zygotic meiosis occurs when meiosis takes place after fertilization, specifically during the formation of haploid cells from a diploid zygote. In this type of meiosis, the zygote undergoes meiosis to produce haploid cells, which then germinate into new organisms.

blocks.title: General Characteristics of Bryophyta
blocks.text:
• Bryophytes include the various mosses and liverworts that are found commonly growing in moist and shaded areas in the hills.
  • Mosses along with lichens are the first organisms to colonise rocks and hence, are of great ecological importance.
  • Main plant body of bryophytes are Gametophyte(n)
  • Sex organs are formed on gametophyte. Sex organs are multicellular and jacketed in bryophytes.Male-Anthridium(n) Female- Archegonium(n)
  • Bryophytes are first embryophytes.
  • In  liverwort asexual reproduction takes place by specialised structures called gemmae

blocks.title: Introduction of Pteridophyta
blocks.text:
Pteridophyte Ptero = wings (Feathers), phyta - plants

  • They are beautiful non-seeded first vascular plants on the earth.
  • Pteridophytes include psilotum, club mosses, horse tails, and Ferns.
  • Pteridophytes are not completely successful land plants because they also need water for fertilization.

blocks.title: General Characteristics of Pteridophyta
blocks.text:
• Present in cool, damp, shady places
  • Some of them flourish in sandy soil
  • First vascular plant group
  • Organs have developed vascular tissue
  • Used as medicinal purposes, ornamental plant and soil binders.
Pteridophytes are two types on the basis of types of spores :

1. Homosporous:- produce only single type of spores eg- most of pteridophyte

2. Heterosporous:-produce two types of spores microspore and megaspore eg- Selaginella, Salvinia

blocks.title: Question-1
blocks.question:
In bryophytes and pteridophytes, transport of male gametes requires :-

(1) Wind

(2) Insects

(3) Birds

(4) Water
blocks.answer:
Ans-(4)

Explanation:

In both bryophytes (e.g., mosses) and pteridophytes (e.g., ferns), the transport of male gametes (sperm) requires water. This is because the sperm need to swim through a thin layer of water to reach the female gametes (egg) for fertilization.

  • Bryophytes and pteridophytes are non-flowering plants that rely on external water (like rain or dew) for the fertilization process.
  • In these plants, water is essential for the sperm to travel to the egg in the archegonium (female reproductive organ).

blocks.title: Question-2
blocks.question:
Genera like Selaginella and Salvinia produce two kinds of spores. Such plants are known as?

(1) Homosorus

(2) Heterosorus

(3) Homosporous

(4) Heterosporous
blocks.answer:
Ans-(4)

Explanation:

  • Heterosporous plants, like Selaginella and Salvinia, produce two distinct types of spores: microspores (small, male spores) and megaspores (large, female spores).
  • This differentiation of spores is a characteristic of heterospory, which is seen in some ferns, lycophytes, and some seed plants.

blocks.title: Question-3
blocks.question:
Gemmae are present in :

(1) Mosses

(2) Pteridophytes

(3) Some Gymnosperms

(4) Some Liverworts
blocks.answer:
Ans-(4)

Explanation:

  • Gemmae are small, multicellular structures used for asexual reproduction in some liverworts. These structures are typically produced in specialized structures called gemma cups.
  • When gemmae are dispersed and land in a suitable environment, they can grow into new liverwort plants.

blocks.title: Question-4
blocks.question:
From an evolutionary point of view, retention of the female gametophyte with a developing young embryo on the parent sporophyte for sometimes, is first observed in?

(1) Liverworts

(2) Mosses

(3) Pteridophytes

(4) Gymnosperms
blocks.answer:
Ans-(4)

Explanation:

  • The retention of the female gametophyte and the developing young embryo on the parent sporophyte for variable period is a significant evolutionary adaptation observed first in pteridophyte.

blocks.title: Introduction of Gymnosperms
blocks.text: • The gymnosperms (gymnos = naked, sperma = seed) and plants in which the ovules are not enclosed by the ovary wall and remain exposed, both before and after fertilization.

blocks.title: General Characteristics
blocks.text:
• First completely successful terrestrial plants.
  • The main plant body of gymnosperm is sporophyte which divided in to root, stem and leaves.
  • Gymnosperms include medium-sized trees or tall trees and shrubs. One of the gymnosperms the giant redwood tree Sequoia is one of the tallest tree species.
  • In gymnosperm embryo & seed formation takes place but no fruit formation.
  • All gymnosperms are vascular plants. Their xylem lacks vessels & phloem lacks sieve tubes and companion cells.
  • The leaves in gymnosperms are well-adapted to extreme conditions like temperature, humidity and wind.
  • Gymnosperm may be monoecious eg-Pinus or Dioecious eg - Cycas.
  • Two types of sporophylls form male cone and female cone respectively.The cones or strobili may form loose or compact cones
  • In bryophytes and pteridophytes, the male and female gametophytes have an independent free-living existence but in gymnosperm both are dependent on sporophytic plant body

blocks.title: Question -1
blocks.question:
Select the correct statement.

(1) Gymnosperms are both homosporous and heterosporous

(2) Salvinia, Ginkgo and Pinus all are gymnosperms

(3) Sequoia is one of the tallest trees

(4) The leaves of gymnosperms are not well adapted to extremes of climate
blocks.answer:
Ans- (3)

Explanation:

  • Gymnosperms are both homosporous and heterosporous (1):
  • Salvinia, Ginkgo, and Pinus all are gymnosperms (2):
  • Sequoia is one of the tallest trees (3):
  • The leaves of gymnosperms are not well adapted to extremes of climate (4):
options: (1) Gymnosperms are both homosporous and heterosporous
(2) Salvinia, Ginkgo and Pinus all are gymnosperms
(3) Sequoia is one of the tallest trees
(4) The leaves of gymnosperms are not well adapted to extremes of climate

blocks.title: Question-2
blocks.question:
Select the mismatch

(1) Cycas – Dioecious

(2) Salvinia – Heterosporous

(3) Equisetum – Homosporous

(4) Pinus – Dioecious

blocks.title: Question-3
blocks.question:
Phloem in gymnosperms lacks :

(1) Albuminous cells and sieve cells

(2) Sieve tubes only

(3) Companion cells only

(4) Both sieve tubes and companion cells
blocks.answer:
Ans-(4)

Explanation:

  • Phloem in gymnosperms lacks sievetube and companion cells. Instead, they have albuminous cells, which function similarly to companion cells but are structurally different.
options: (4) Both sieve tubes and companion cells
